title: Talking about God (ST I.13)
hook: God is good, but not in exactly the way we are good

segments.voice: Yesterday, simplicity: God has no parts, and in God what God is and that God is are one. Your line was no parts. When did you stop and do one thing, whole? Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

A girl back from her first trip to the coast is on the phone with a friend from inland, who has never seen the sea. It's like the lake, she says. But bigger. No, way bigger, you can't see the other side. And it moves by itself. And it's salty. And it's loud. She keeps reaching for words her friend already has, and every one is true, and every one falls short. Thomas Aquinas has the same problem, only harder. Every word we have, we learned from things around us. So when anyone says God is good, or wise, what can those words possibly mean? Today's word is his answer.
screen: `A GIRL DESCRIBES THE SEA.` → `LIKE THE LAKE, BUT BIGGER.` → `WHAT CAN OUR WORDS MEAN?`

segments.voice: Thomas sees two dead ends. The first: our words mean exactly the same of God as of us. God is good the way a kind neighbor is good, just more so. But then God is one more thing among things, only larger, and yesterday we heard Thomas say God isn't built like anything we know. The second dead end: our words mean something totally different of God, the way a river bank and a savings bank share only a spelling. But then, Thomas says, we could know nothing about God at all, and every argument we've walked would be empty. So he takes a middle road, and calls it analogy. His own example is the word healthy. A person is healthy. A meal is healthy, because it brings health. A face looks healthy, because it shows health. Same word, not the same meaning, and not unrelated either. Each use points to the one health. Now, God is good. Thomas insists this doesn't merely mean God causes good things, or isn't bad. It means goodness is really in God, in a higher way. And then he flips the whole picture. We learn the word good from good things around us, so it feels as if the word belongs to us first. But as to what it means, Thomas says, it belongs to God first, and to us by sharing. He points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, praying to the Father "of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named." We learned father from our fathers. Paul says fatherhood is named from God. So, for Thomas, our words aren't wrong about God. They're true, and they're too small. God is like what they say, and more.
screen: `NOT THE SAME SENSE.` · `NOT A TOTALLY DIFFERENT SENSE.` · `LIKE THE WORD HEALTHY.` · `GOD'S FIRST, OURS BY SHARING.` · then, large: `OF WHOM ALL PATERNITY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing God is like, and unlike. Settle, and breathe. Pick one word you'd use of God, or of whatever is largest in your life. Good. Faithful. Father. Light. Hold the word, and remember where you first learned it: a person, a morning, a kitchen. Let it be true. Then let it stretch. Where does your memory of that word fall short? Where would it have to be more? Stay between the two, like and unlike, without closing the gap. If you pray, you can speak the word quietly to God, and let it be too small. The bell holds the time.
Analogy. Thomas Aquinas's way of speaking of God: our words are not used in exactly the same sense, nor a totally different one, but a related one. True, and more. Today's word.
Your line: like, and more. Today, when you call something good, notice where the word came from, and where it might be pointing. Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Catholic theology uses Thomas's teaching on analogy to explain how words like good, wise and father can be said truly of God while God remains beyond them; readers meet it in the Summa's question on the names of God.

match.prompt: talking about God — tap the pairs.

myth: Thomas says 'God is good' only means God causes good things
he says goodness is really in God, in a higher way.
Thomas says words like good and wise mean exactly the same of God as of us
not the same sense, and not a totally different one: an analogy.
Thomas says that, as to what they mean, such words belong to God first
we learn them from creatures first, but the reality is God's first; Paul says all fatherhood is named from God.

fork.setup: someone says, God is good. what does Thomas think those words can mean?
options: good in exactly the way a kind neighbor is good, only bigger.
good in a sense with no link to our goodness at all.
truly good, like our goodness, and beyond it.
fork.reveal: Thomas rejects both the same sense and a totally different sense. the word is used by analogy: true of God, in a higher way, and God's first.

original.note: Latin, from Greek: proportion — Thomas says names are said of God and creatures by analogy, that is, by proportion.

trapdoor: what you thought: words about God are either literal or just poetry.
what it means: our words reach God truly, but God is always more than they hold: like, and more.
what a scholar hears: not univocal, not equivocal, but analogical, by proportion; what the word signifies belongs to God first, the way of signifying is ours.

sources.quoted: of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named

notes: ST I.13 paraphrased: a.2 'God is good' is said substantially, not merely as cause or as negation; goodness pre-exists in God in a higher way; a.3 thing signified versus mode of signifying; a.5 names said neither univocally nor purely equivocally but by analogy, 'that is, according to proportion', with 'healthy' as the example (Thomas's examples are animal, medicine and urine; the script uses person, meal and face); a.6 as to the thing signified, names are said primarily of God, citing Ephesians 3:15. Confirm.
The sea, the river bank and savings bank are the script's illustrations, not Thomas's.
Douay-Rheims Ephesians 3:15: confirm exact wording ('Of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named').
Original: Thomas's phrase is 'secundum analogiam, idest proportionem'; the note says 'from Greek: proportion'. Confirm.
